title: Shares and how they work
blurb: What owning a share means, how it can pay you, and what moves its price.
t1.title: Owning a piece
t1.hook: Chaiwala Ltd runs tea stalls. Its ownership is cut into {tot} equal pieces called shares. Asha buys {mine} of them. Your mission: understand what she now owns.
t1.define: A **share**, also called a stock, is a small piece of ownership in a company. Owners can earn in two ways: when the price rises, and from a **dividend**.
t1.analogy: Imagine a tea stall cut into 1,000 equal parts. Each part owns a tiny share of the stall, its profit and its future.
q1.prompt: What does owning a share mean?
q1.opt.a: You own a small part of the company
q1.opt.b: You have lent money to the company
q1.opt.d: You now work for the company
q1.hint: Think about the stall cut into equal parts.
q1.explain: A share is a small piece of ownership. It is not a loan, and it guarantees nothing.
q2.prompt: A company has {t2} shares and you own {m2} of them. What percentage of the company do you own? Type a percentage.
q2.hint: Your shares divided by all the shares.
q2.explain: {m2} out of {t2} is {own} of the company.
t2.title: Two ways to earn
t2.define: A share can pay you in two ways. The price can rise, which is a price gain. The company can pay a **dividend**, a part of its profit shared with owners. Fees reduce what you keep.
t2.explore: Open the lab. It shows 10 shares bought at a fixed price. Change the price and the dividend, then answer the questions.
q3.prompt: In the lab, set the price change to +{chgQ} and the dividend to {divQ} per share. What is your total profit? Type a number in rupees.
q3.hint: Read your profit under the lab. It counts the price gain and the dividend, and takes off the fee.
q3.explain: The shares are worth {nowPrice} each. After the dividend and the {fee} fee, the profit is {profitLab}.
q4.prompt: With the same settings, how much dividend did you receive in total? Type a number in rupees.
q4.hint: Read the dividend received in the lab.
q5.prompt: Which of these is a dividend?
q5.opt.a: A part of the profit that a company pays out to its owners
q5.opt.b: The fee you pay to buy a share
q5.opt.c: The rise in a share's price
q5.opt.d: The total value of the company
q5.hint: Read the definition at the top of this task.
q5.explain: A dividend is a part of the profit paid out to owners. It is separate from the price.
t3.title: What moves a price
t3.define: Share prices move with news, results and mood. Good news can lift a price. Bad news can lower it. Nobody can promise which way it will go.
t3.tradeoff: Owners can gain more than lenders, but they are paid last if the company fails. Prices can swing, and an owner can lose the whole amount.
q6.prompt: Chaiwala opens 20 new stalls, which is good news. What can you say about its share price?
q6.opt.a: It may rise, but there is no guarantee
q6.opt.d: It will fall, because news always hurts
q6.fb.b: Good news can lift a price, but other things move it too, and the news may already be in the price. Nothing here is guaranteed.
q6.hint: Reread the first card. Can anyone promise a direction?
q6.explain: News can lift a price, but nobody can promise it.
q7.prompt: If a company fails, who is paid first?
q7.opt.a: The owners, because they own it
q7.hint: Remember the lending and bonds rooms. Who has a promise to be paid back?
q7.explain: Lenders are paid before owners. Owners can gain more, but they carry more risk.
t4.title: Company size
t4.define: **Market cap** is the share price multiplied by the number of shares. It shows how big a company is. A low share price does not mean a small company.
t4.mistake: Many people think a higher share price means a bigger or better company. It does not. You must look at the number of shares too.
q8.prompt: Company A has a share price of {priceA} and {sharesA} shares. What is its market cap? Type a number in rupees.
q8.hint: Price × number of shares. The result is large, so check your zeros.
q9.prompt: Company A has a share price of {priceA} and 2,000,000 shares. Company B has a share price of {priceB} and 10,000 shares. Which is the bigger company?
q9.opt.b: Company B, because its share price is higher
q9.fb.b: The price of one share does not show the size of the company. Count all the shares too.
q9.hint: Work out the market cap of both and compare.
q9.explain: A is worth {capA} and B only {capB}. The cheaper share belongs to the bigger company.
t5.title: Exchanges and prices
t5.define: An **exchange** is a regulated marketplace where buyers and sellers meet. The **bid** is the highest price a buyer offers. The **ask** is the lowest price a seller wants. The gap between them is the **spread**.
t5.define2: **Liquidity** is how easily you can sell without moving the price. A share with few buyers is hard to sell quickly at a fair price.
q10.prompt: A share has a bid of {bid} and an ask of {ask}. What is the spread? Type a number in rupees.
q11.prompt: A share has very few buyers, so selling it quickly means accepting a lower price. This is called…
q11.explain: Few buyers means the share is hard to sell without losing on price. That is low liquidity.
glossary.share.def: A small piece of ownership in a company.
glossary.dividend.def: A part of a company's profit paid out to its owners.
glossary.exchange.def: A regulated marketplace where buyers and sellers trade.
glossary.market_cap.def: Share price multiplied by the number of shares.
glossary.bid.def: The highest price a buyer is offering.
glossary.ask.def: The lowest price a seller will accept.
glossary.spread.def: The gap between the ask and the bid.
glossary.liquidity.def: How easily something can be sold without moving its price.
